statement: Legacy code is code without tests; the presence or absence of tests, not authorship or age, is the working definition that points to a solution.
Code without tests is bad code no matter how well written, object-oriented, or well-encapsulated it is, because without tests you cannot verifiably change its behavior.
With tests in place a team can change code behavior quickly and verifiably; without tests the team cannot know whether a change makes the code better or worse.
Making large changes to code without supporting tests is dangerous, and clean, well-structured code alone does not remove that risk.
Designs that cannot tolerate changing requirements are poor designs; creating designs that tolerate change is the goal of every competent software developer.
Preventing code rot is imperfect: even disciplined teams using the best principles, patterns, and practices still create messes, so teams must be able to reverse rot, not only prevent it.

In legacy code, good design is reached in discrete incremental steps; some steps taken to make code changeable may temporarily make parts of the code slightly uglier, and best must not become the enemy of better.
The dependency-breaking techniques are meant to be applied without tests, as a means of getting tests in place.
condition: when the goal is to put initial tests around legacy code

statement: There are four primary reasons to change software: adding a feature, fixing a bug, improving the design, and optimizing resource usage.
Behavior is the most important thing about software because it is what users depend on; adding wanted behavior builds trust, while changing or removing behavior users rely on erodes it.
Adding new code and calling it usually adds behavior, whereas modifying existing code can change behavior, so the two kinds of change carry different risk.
Adding a method to a class does not change the system's behavior unless the method is actually called.
Refactoring is improving the internal structure of software without changing its external behavior, done as a series of small structural modifications supported by tests.

Refactoring differs from general cleanup: it is neither low-risk work like reformatting source nor invasive risky work like rewriting chunks, but small structural changes backed by tests to make code easier to change.
Optimization keeps a program's functionality exactly the same while changing a resource it consumes, usually time or memory.
Unintentionally dropping or altering behavior while improving a system's design is a bug.
Three things can change when work is done in a system: structure, functionality, and resource usage.
Adding a feature, refactoring, and optimizing all hold existing functionality invariant, and even bug fixing changes only a small amount of functionality relative to what is preserved.
In every kind of software change, far more behavior must be preserved than is intentionally changed.
Preserving existing behavior is one of the largest challenges in software development.
The hard part of preserving behavior is not its volume but not knowing how much of the behavior is at risk when a change is made.
Understanding is the key thing needed to make changes safely.
To mitigate the risk of a change, answer three questions: what changes must be made, how will we know we made them correctly, and how will we know we have not broken anything.
Minimizing the number of changes to reduce risk backfires: avoided classes and methods grow larger and harder to understand.
Avoiding change makes developers rusty at it, so involved structural work such as breaking up a large class stays hard instead of becoming routine.
Chronic avoidance of change breeds a team-wide fear of change that grows worse over time.
Software changes are made in two ways: Edit and Pray (plan carefully, make the change, then poke around hoping nothing broke) and Cover and Modify (change under the safety net of tests).
Safety in changing software is not solely a function of care; care without the right tools and techniques is like a surgeon operating with a butter knife.
Covering software with tests catches bad changes quickly and keeps them from leaking out to infect the rest of the system.
Tests can be used two ways: testing to show correctness (traditional, run after development) and testing to detect change (regression testing).
Tests around the area being changed act as a software vise, holding most behavior fixed so that only the intended piece of behavior changes, one piece at a time.
Regression testing is traditionally done at the application interface, but it pays to do it at a finer-grained level.
Fast fine-grained feedback localizes an error to the last small change made, whereas overnight application-level regression runs make localizing a failure slow and ambiguous.
Unit testing is one of the most important components of legacy code work; small localized tests give feedback as you develop and let you refactor with much more safety.
A unit test exercises an individual component in isolation: functions in procedural code, classes in object-oriented code.
Good unit tests run fast and help localize problems.
A unit test that takes a tenth of a second to run is slow; if a test does not run fast, it is not a unit test.
A test is not a unit test if it talks to a database, communicates across a network, touches the file system, or requires special environment setup to run.
exception: such tests are still worth writing, but must be kept separate from the fast unit-test suite

statement: Large tests have three weaknesses: worse error localization, longer execution time (so they end up not being run), and a harder-to-see connection between code and the values that exercise it.
Higher-level tests have a place: they pin down the behavior of a set of classes at once, which then makes it easier to write tests for the individual classes.
Given a choice, it is always safer to put tests around a change before making it, because covering code with tests first makes mistakes more likely to be caught.
Difficulty creating an object or running a method in a test harness is a dependency problem: classes that depend directly on things hard to use in a test are hard to modify and hard to work with.
Dependency is one of the most critical problems in software development, and much legacy code work consists of breaking dependencies so that change becomes easier.
The Legacy Code Dilemma: to change code safely you should have tests in place, but to put tests in place you often have to change the code first.

Resolve the Legacy Code Dilemma by breaking dependencies (for example extracting an interface or passing only what a method really needs) to get tests in place, and perform those initial dependency-breaking refactorings very conservatively.
condition: when getting legacy code under test

statement: Breaking dependencies to get code under test may temporarily make the code look poorer, like incision scars; cover the code around those points later to heal them.
The Legacy Code Change Algorithm is: identify change points, find test points, break dependencies, write tests, then make changes and refactor.
The day-to-day goal in legacy code is to make functional changes that deliver value while bringing more of the system under test, so each programming episode yields both new code and its tests.
Use test-driven development (TDD) to add features in legacy code.
Tests written to add a feature often give cover to do some refactoring afterward, once you are better versed in the code's problems.

Refactoring legacy code toward better structure proceeds in baby steps, where better is context-dependent and often just a few steps more maintainable than before, not ideal, clean, or pattern-enriched.
Even simple, mechanical improvements such as breaking down a large class to make it easier to work with can make a significant difference in an application.
Dependencies among classes can make it very hard to get clusters of objects under test, because creating one object can transitively require nearly the whole system.

There are two reasons to break dependencies to get tests in place: sensing, when you cannot access values your code computes, and separation, when you cannot even get a piece of code into a test harness to run.
There are many techniques for separating software but one dominant technique for sensing, namely faking the collaborator.
A fake object impersonates a collaborator of the class under test, letting the test sense effects through it.
To make a collaborator fakeable, introduce a seam such as extracting an interface so the class under test can hold either the real collaborator or a fake, then test against the fake.
A unit test that uses a fake still tells you how the unit affects its collaborator, which helps localize errors even though it does not exercise the fully integrated system.
Writing tests for individual units yields small, well-understood pieces, which makes it easier to reason about the code.

A fake object has two sides: the interface method the production class sees, and inspection methods used only by the test, so the test should hold the fake as its concrete type to reach those inspection methods.
In non-object-oriented languages, implement a fake by defining an alternative function that records values in a global data structure the test can access.
condition: when working in a non-object-oriented language

statement: A mock object is a fake that performs assertions internally: you set the calls it should expect, exercise it, then call verify to check the expectations were met.
Prefer simple fake objects over mock frameworks: mock frameworks are not available in all languages, and simple fakes suffice in most situations.
Code is generally poorly suited to testing, and the reliable ways to end up with an easily testable program are to write tests as you develop it or to deliberately design for testability.
Reuse is hard: even software pieces that look independent often depend on each other in subtle ways.
Pulling classes out of an existing project for unit testing usually forces you to break many dependencies regardless of how good the design is, and doing so changes your idea of what good design is.
A seam is a place where you can alter behavior in your program without editing in that place.
An object seam lets you change the method that is called without changing the method that calls it, and object seams are available in object-oriented languages.

The seam view helps you spot testing opportunities already in the code: at seams you can selectively exclude dependencies or run substitute code to sense conditions, getting just enough tests in place to support more aggressive work.
The kinds of seams available depend on the steps that turn program text into running code, and each identifiable step exposes different kinds of seams, such as preprocessing seams in C and C++.

Excessive preprocessing in production code decreases clarity, because conditional-compilation directives force maintaining several programs in one source and macros do blind text replacement that can hide obscure bugs.
Every seam has an enabling point: a place, separate from the seam itself, where you decide which of the two behaviors is used.
The source code should be identical in production and test; you exploit a seam by changing behavior at its enabling point, not by editing at the seam location.

A link seam exploits the reference-resolution or linking step to substitute a different implementation, for example an alternate class on the classpath in Java or a separate test library linked by the build in static C or C++.
The enabling point for a link seam is always outside the program text, often in a build or deployment script, which makes link seams somewhat hard to notice.
If you use link seams, make the difference between the test and production environments obvious.
condition: when using link seams

statement: When stubbing a tell-style interface via a link seam, stub functions can be empty; if the functions return values, return a success code or the default value of the type.
Sensing through a link seam takes more work than separation: you record the calls in a data structure that the test can later inspect.
Start a sensing scheme very simple and let it grow only as complicated as it needs to be to meet the current sensing need.

In object-oriented languages a method call does not by itself determine which method executes; if you can change which method is called without editing the code around the call, that call is an object seam.

Not every method call is an object seam: a call has no seam when it has no enabling point, such as when the object is constructed in the same method so its class cannot be varied without editing that method.
Passing a collaborator in as a parameter creates an object seam whose enabling point is the argument list, letting a test supply any subtype to change behavior without editing the calling method.
A call to a static or private method can be turned into an object seam by removing static and making the method protected, so a testing subclass can override it.

In particularly nasty legacy code, modify the code as little as possible while getting tests in place; knowing the seams your language offers lets you get tests in place more safely than editing the code directly.

Choose the right seam type: object seams are generally best in object-oriented languages, while preprocessing and link seams are less explicit and their tests can be hard to maintain, so reserve them for pervasive dependencies with no better alternative.
Once you get used to seeing code in terms of seams, it becomes easier to see how to test things and how to structure new code to make testing easier.
The tools needed for legacy code work are an editor or IDE, a build system, and a testing framework, plus refactoring tools for your language when available.
Refactoring is a change made to the internal structure of software to make it easier to understand and cheaper to modify without changing its existing behavior.
A change is a refactoring only if it does not change behavior; refactoring tools should verify that a change preserves behavior, and tools that do not check can introduce subtle bugs.

Choose refactoring tools with care: find out what the developers say about the tool's safety and run your own sanity checks, such as whether extracting a method with the name of an existing or base-class method is flagged.
If a tool's automated refactorings do not preserve behavior, do not use them; follow the advice for working without a refactoring tool, which is safer.

Automated refactoring without tests is safe only when you go from one verified-safe automated refactoring directly to another with no other editing, and even then some tool refactorings (such as inlining a variable that hides a side effect) can silently change behavior.
condition: when going directly from one safe automated refactoring to another with no manual edits

statement: It is a good idea to have tests around code before using automated refactorings; you can refactor without tests only if you know exactly what the tool checks and what it does not.
When adopting a new refactoring tool, first put its extract-method support through its paces; if you can trust it without tests, you can use it to get code into a more testable state.

User-interface-based testing tools are often more work than expected and a poor place to write tests, because UIs are volatile and far from the functionality under test, so UI-based test failures are hard to diagnose.

The xUnit unit-testing framework has three key features: programmers write tests in the language they develop in, all tests run in isolation, and tests can be grouped into suites to be run and rerun on demand.
In JUnit you write tests by subclassing TestCase, and each method with the signature void testXXX() defines a test containing code and assertions.
The xUnit runner creates a completely separate object for each test method, so tests cannot affect one another.

A setUp method runs before each test method to build that test's objects freshly, and a tearDown method runs after; deferring allocation to setUp saves resources and lets setup problems be detected and reported.
The FIT framework lets specifiers embed input and output tables in HTML documents that the framework runs as tests, giving users and developers a common, up-to-date view of the system's capabilities.

Breaking dependencies and writing tests before a change costs time up front but usually saves time and frustration overall, because it avoids unknown debugging time and makes functional problems easier to nail down.
Changes cluster in systems: if you are changing a piece of code today, you will likely have a change nearby soon, so an investment in testability is usually recouped.
A useful team experiment is, for one iteration, to make no change without tests covering it, and to hold a quick group meeting whenever someone believes a test cannot be written.
Code is your house and you have to live in it, so quick decisions to skip tests under pressure carry a lasting cost.
In legacy code it is particularly hard to produce meaningful estimates of how long a change will take.
When you have to change a class under time pressure, first try instantiating it in a test harness, because getting the code under test is often easier than you expect.
If you genuinely cannot break dependencies and get tests in place now, scrutinize whether the change can instead be made by writing fresh code that you can test.
Techniques that add new tested code without covering the calling code test the new code but not its use, so they must be used with caution.

Sprout Method: when a feature can be formulated completely as new code, write it in a new method and call it from where the functionality is needed, so you can test the new method even when the call sites are not easily testable.
condition: when the added feature can be formulated as new code

statement: Sprout Method separates new code from old, giving a clean interface and visible variable effects, whereas adding the code inline mingles concerns and muddies the method.
Prefer Sprout Method over adding code inline whenever the added code is a distinct piece of work or you cannot yet get tests around the method.
The disadvantage of Sprout Method is that you temporarily give up on getting the source method and its class under test and improving them, leaving the source in a slightly odd state.
When bad dependencies prevent instantiating a class to sprout a method, consider Pass Null, or make the sprout a public static method that takes the needed instance variables as arguments.
condition: when the class cannot be instantiated in a test harness

statement: Static methods on a class can act as a staging area: once several statics share the same variables, you can often extract a new class and move them over as instance methods.

Sprout Class: when you cannot create objects of a class in a test harness within a reasonable time because of heavy creational or hidden dependencies, put your change in a new class that the source class uses.
condition: when the class cannot be brought into a test harness in reasonable time

statement: Develop a sprouted method or class test-first, and write the call to it first (commented out) so you can see how the call reads in context before implementing the code.

A sprouted class may later fold into existing concepts through a shared interface or become a new concept of its own, so do not hold back from sprouting just because the class seems insignificant at first.

Two situations lead to Sprout Class: the change adds an entirely new responsibility that is off to the side of the class's main responsibility, or a small piece of functionality belongs in an existing class that you cannot get into a test harness.

The key advantage of Sprout Class is that it lets you move forward with more confidence than making invasive changes, and in C++ it also avoids modifying existing headers, which decreases the compilation load on the source class.
The key disadvantage of Sprout Class is conceptual complexity: work that ideally would have stayed in one class ends up in sprouts, gutting the abstractions, just to make safe change possible.
Adding behavior directly to an existing method is easy but often wrong: code added only because it must execute at the same time creates temporal coupling, and excessive temporal coupling is harmful.

Grouping operations only because they happen at the same time forms a weak relationship; if you later need one without the other, they may have grown together and, without a seam, separating them is hard work.

Wrap Method (rename form): rename the original method and create a new method with the same name and signature that calls the renamed old code plus the new behavior, preserving signatures so existing callers are unaffected.
Wrap Method (new-method form): develop the new behavior as a new method, then create another method that calls both the new and the old method, used when nothing calls the new behavior yet.
Wrap Method applies only when the new feature can run entirely before or after the old feature and is not intertwined with the old logic.
condition: the new behavior can be placed entirely before or after the old behavior

statement: Wrap Method gets new tested functionality into an application without increasing the size of existing methods, and it makes the new functionality explicitly independent of the existing functionality.
The primary disadvantage of Wrap Method is that it can lead to poor names, because you must invent a new name for the renamed old code.
Wrap Class adds new behavior to a system by placing it in another class that uses the method, rather than in the existing class.
To wrap a class you cannot instantiate in a test harness, use Extract Implementer or Extract Interface on it so the wrapper can implement that interface.
condition: when the wrapped class cannot be instantiated in a test harness

statement: In the decorator pattern a wrapper class shares the same interface as the class it wraps so clients cannot tell, delegates to the wrapped object, and lets you build up complex behavior by composing objects at runtime.

To apply decorator, define an abstract decorator class that implements the operations and delegates to a held instance, subclass it to override methods and add behavior, and provide at least one concrete non-decorator base class to wrap around.
Use the decorator pattern sparingly, because decorators that decorate other decorators are hard to navigate, like peeling the layers of an onion.
When the new behavior is needed in only one or a few places, use a plain, non-decorator wrapper class that performs the work and the new behavior and is instantiated only where needed.
Choose a decorator-style wrapper when many callers must get the new behavior at once, and a plain wrapper when the behavior is needed in only a couple of places.

Use Sprout Method when the existing method already communicates a clear algorithm, and move to Wrap Method when the new feature is as important as the existing work, which yields a new high-level algorithm in the wrapping method.

Two cases tip toward Wrap Class: the new behavior is completely independent and you do not want to pollute the class with low-level or unrelated behavior, or the class has grown so large that you wrap just to put a stake in the ground and provide a roadmap for later changes.
The biggest obstacle to improvement in a large code base is what the existing ugly code leads you to believe: that it will always be ugly and that any small improvement is not worth it.
Consistently making small improvements transforms a system over a couple of months, even though the initial steps can look silly or make the code temporarily more complicated.

Make-changes-without-tests techniques trade off: sometimes they move toward better design by separating new responsibilities from old, and sometimes a class exists only because the team was not prepared to take the time to get the existing class under test.
As the amount of code in a project grows it gradually surpasses understanding, and the time it takes to figure out what to change keeps increasing.

In a well-maintained system a change is usually easy once you figure out how to make it, whereas in a legacy system figuring it out takes long and the change is difficult too, leaving you with only narrow understanding.
Systems broken up into small, well-named, understandable pieces enable faster work.
Lag time is the amount of time between making a change and getting real feedback about it; long lag time makes development slow and inefficient, like driving a rover on Mars from Earth.

Bundling many changes to avoid building often is usually unnecessary waste, because in most mainstream languages you can break dependencies so that you recompile and run tests against the code you are working on in under ten seconds.
You should be able to compile every class or module in your system separately from the others and in its own test harness, which gives very rapid feedback and speeds development.

Compressing feedback time from a minute to a few seconds changes the quality of mental work: you use feedback to try approaches quickly, concentrate more intensely, and notice and correct mistakes much faster.
For developers in compiled languages, the main impediment to rapid feedback is dependency: the need to compile something you do not care about just to compile something you do.
To break dependencies in object-oriented code, first try to instantiate the needed classes in a test harness, which in the easiest cases requires only importing or including their declarations.
When a class is huge or has overwhelming dependencies, it can pay to cut out a larger chunk of code and put that under test at a pinch point, a place where writing tests is easier.
A method's own execution cost is usually low compared with the cost of the external resources its called methods touch, such as the database, hardware, or communications infrastructure.
exception: except when the methods are very calculation-intensive

statement: To speed builds for a cluster of classes, find the dependencies in the way by trying to use the classes in a test harness, since nearly every problem you hit will be a dependency you should break.
Extract interfaces for the classes in a cluster that are used from outside the cluster, so external classes depend on the interface rather than the concrete class.

In C++, Extract Implementer is a little easier than Extract Interface because you do not have to rename references throughout, though you must change the places that create instances of the old class.

When a class depends on an interface rather than a concrete class, it recompiles only if the interface changes, and interfaces change far less often than the code behind them, which creates a compilation firewall.

Prefer to depend on interfaces or abstract classes rather than concrete classes, because depending on less volatile things minimizes the chance that a particular change triggers massive recompilation.
Moving cohesive class clusters into their own package or library behind interfaces raises the total full-rebuild cost slightly but can dramatically reduce the average incremental build time.

Fast rebuild-and-test cycles give greater feedback as you develop, meaning fewer errors and less aggravation, and the conceptual overhead of more interfaces and packages is a fair price to pay for it.
Getting a set of classes compiling separately and under test is a one-time cost per set, after which you reap the benefits indefinitely.
Sprouting and wrapping without tests has hazards beyond the obvious: the existing code does not get better, and the added code can duplicate code in untested areas and fester unnoticed.
Fear and resignation are hazards of avoiding change, because fear gets in the way of good decision-making and the sprouts and wraps left in the code are reminders of it.
It is generally better to confront the beast than to hide from it: get the code under test and then add features on a solid foundation.

Test-driven development is the most powerful feature-addition technique: imagine a method that solves part of the problem and write a failing test for it, which solidifies your understanding of what the code should do before you write it.
The TDD algorithm is: write a failing test case, get it to compile, make it pass, remove duplication, and repeat.
TDD steps are typically much smaller than writing the whole implementation; write a large amount of code in response to one test only when you are certain of the algorithm you need.
When getting a TDD test to compile, do not get lost generalizing; make it compile now, even by copying and renaming, and generalize later only if you still want to.

Copying code and modifying it in a new method is powerful in legacy code because you can see your modifications side by side with the old code and later either remove the duplication or discard the attempt.

Removing duplication is the critical final TDD step: adding features by copying blocks is acceptable only if you then remove the duplication, or you create a maintenance burden, and having tests in place makes removing duplication easy.

TDD lets you concentrate on one thing at a time, writing code or refactoring but never both at once, which is especially valuable in legacy code because you write new code independently and then refactor to remove duplication with the old.
The TDD algorithm for legacy code adds a step zero, get the class you want to change under test first, and during the make-it-pass step you should try not to change existing code.

Test-driven development is not tied to object orientation; in object-oriented code you also have programming by difference, using inheritance to introduce a feature without modifying a class directly, then deciding how to integrate it.

Programming by difference adds a feature quickly through a subclass that overrides a method, and using inheritance initially does not mean keeping it, because with tests you can move to other structures if the inheritance becomes problematic.
A test that pins down new behavior lets you preserve that behavior while you later change the design.
A big problem with extensive inheritance is that if you put features into distinct subclasses, you can only have one of those features at a time and cannot combine them.

To combine features that were added by subclassing, stop before adding the second feature and refactor, for example turning the variation into a configuration option, using the existing tests to verify behavior is preserved.
When conditional statements from many properties start to litter a class, replace the properties collection with a dedicated class that holds it and provides higher-level functionality.
Move behavior onto the collaborator or configuration class so it owns the decision, and rename that class when it stops being passive, so the name reflects its real responsibility.
Rename Class is the most powerful refactoring, because it changes the way people see the code and lets them notice possibilities they had not considered.

The Liskov Substitution Principle says objects of a subclass should be substitutable for objects of their superclass throughout the code, and violations such as Square extending Rectangle cause silent errors.

The Liskov Substitution Principle implies clients should be able to use a subclass object without knowing it is a subclass, and there is no mechanical way to fully avoid violations because conformance depends on the clients and what they expect.

Two rules of thumb help avoid Liskov Substitution Principle violations: whenever possible avoid overriding concrete methods, and if you do, call the method you are overriding from within the overriding method.
Overriding concrete methods too often makes code confusing, because a reader looking at the superclass method may not realize that a subclass override is the code actually executed.

In a normalized hierarchy no class overrides a concrete method it inherited, so each class has at most one implementation of a method and the question of how a class does something is answered by looking at that class or its abstract method's subclass implementation.
To keep inheritance safely, make the superclass abstract with an abstract method and let subclasses provide the concrete bodies, moving the design toward a normalized hierarchy.

A few concrete overrides now and then are fine as long as they do not cause a Liskov Substitution Principle violation, but it is good to periodically consider how far classes are from normalized form and move toward it when separating responsibilities.

The four most common problems getting a class into a test harness are: objects of the class cannot be created easily, the test harness will not build with the class in it, the constructor has bad side effects, and significant work happens in the constructor that you need to sense.
The best way to find out whether a class will be hard to instantiate in a test harness is to just try it: write a test that attempts to create the object and let the compiler tell you what is needed.
A construction test simply tries to create the object, usually with no assertion; once you can construct the object, discard or rename the test to exercise something more substantial.

When a real collaborator is an irritating parameter, such as a network connection that is slow or unreliable in tests, extract an interface on it and pass a fake that supplies the values the code under test needs.
condition: when a required constructor parameter is slow, unreliable, or has side effects under test

statement: Test code does not have to meet the same standards as production code, so breaking encapsulation with public variables or empty and null-returning fake methods is acceptable to make testing easier, but test code should still be clean, easy to understand, and easy to change.
Duplicated setup lines shared across tests should be extracted into the test class's setUp method.

Pass Null: passing null for a constructor parameter that the code under test does not use is acceptable in tests, because if the code does use it the runtime throws and the harness catches the exception, so you find out quickly.
condition: in tests, when the parameter is not exercised by the code under test

statement: Needing null checks and conditional null-handling scattered throughout a system is a symptom of a nasty system.

Pass Null works in languages that throw when a null reference is used at runtime, such as Java and C#, but is unsafe in C and C++ unless the runtime detects null-pointer errors, where tests may crash mysteriously or be silently wrong and corrupt memory.
condition: in languages that throw when null references are used at runtime
exception: unsafe in C or C++ unless the runtime detects null-pointer errors

statement: Do not pass null in production code unless you have no other choice; when writing fresh code there are better alternatives, such as the Null Object Pattern.
The Null Object Pattern avoids null by returning a special object that does nothing for the operation, shielding clients from explicit null or error checking.

Null objects are useful specifically when a client does not have to care whether an operation succeeded, and must be used cautiously because a null object can silently skew logic such as a paid-employee count.
Subclass and Override Method breaks a dependency by overriding the offending method in a testing subclass, provided you are not altering the behavior you intend to test.
exception: only when the override does not change the behavior under test

statement: A hidden dependency is when a constructor uses a resource you cannot access nicely in a test harness, for example allocating a collaborator with new inside the constructor.
Parameterize Constructor externalizes a constructor's dependency by passing it in, so a test can supply a fake through an extracted interface while a production caller supplies the real object.

Parameterize Constructor need not change every client: extract the constructor body into an initialize method preserving signatures, keep the original constructor delegating to it, and add the parameterized constructor, which is safe to do without tests.

Prefer Parameterize Constructor for hidden constructor dependencies when the object is created in the constructor and has no construction dependencies of its own, because it is then the easiest technique to apply.
condition: when the created object has no construction dependencies of its own

statement: When a constructor creates many objects internally or builds objects from other objects it created, Parameterize Constructor produces a very large parameter list and is not the best choice.

Avoid calling overridable functions from constructors: C++ will not resolve them to derived-class overrides, and in general an overridden function invoked during base construction can access uninitialized base-class variables.

Supersede Instance Variable adds a setter that swaps in another instance after construction; use it sparingly because of resource-management risk, and in C++ take care to correctly delete the replaced object.
Never use a superseding, test-only setter method in production code, because superseded objects that manage resources can cause serious resource problems.

Framework-style reuse, where the framework calls your code, is not the old-style reuse of grabbing a class and using it directly, and you cannot achieve real reuse if you cannot pull a random class out of an application and compile it independently in a test harness without a lot of work.

Global variable usage is one of the hardest dependencies for testing, and global variables are bad partly because of opacity: from a call site you cannot tell what a class accesses or modifies elsewhere.
Globals force you, in a testing situation, to figure out which globals a class uses and set them to the proper state before each test, which is tedious and error-prone.
In Java, the Singleton pattern is one of the mechanisms people use to create global variables.
Each test in a suite should be a mini-application totally isolated from the other tests, so to run code containing singletons under test you must relax the singleton property.
Introduce Static Setter adds a static setTestingInstance method to a singleton so tests can replace its single instance.

Alternatively add a resetForTesting method that nulls the singleton instance and call it in setUp and tearDown to get a fresh singleton per test; this works when the singleton's public methods let you set up its state, otherwise Introduce Static Setter with a subclass override is better.

Distinguish the real reasons to enforce a single instance (modeling one real-world thing, two instances causing a serious problem, or two instances wasting resources) from the common but weak reason of wanting a global variable to avoid passing it around.

If a singleton exists only to serve as a global variable, there is no reason to keep the singleton property, and you can make the constructor protected, public, or package scope and still have a decent, testable system.

When you relax the singleton property, protect against misuse with a team rule, a build-time check that searches sources so setTestingInstance is not called by non-test code, or a runtime check that alarms or suspends if it is called.

To keep part of the singleton property while enabling testing, subclass the singleton and override methods that break dependencies such as database access, and make the base constructor protected so only subclasses, not arbitrary callers, can be created.
When a singleton's dependencies are extensive, use Extract Interface or Extract Implementer on it and change all references to the interface, leaning on the compiler to drive the change.

Introduce Static Setter gets tests in place despite extensive global dependencies but does not remove them; to remove the globals, use Parameterize Method or Parameterize Constructor to trade a global reference for a method temporary or an object field.

Parameterize Method's downside is a proliferation of extra methods that distract readers, while Parameterize Constructor's downside is an extra field per object that the creator must supply, which can raise memory use and often signals other design problems.

If thousands of objects each need a database reference, ask why: separating responsibilities so some classes act and others store and retrieve data localizes dependencies, so not every object needs the reference.
Most global variables are globally accessible but not globally used; they appear in relatively few places, so you can refactor to reduce the global's scope.
A global variable that really is used in every place means there is no layering in the code.

C++'s textual include mechanism reparses each declaration every time it is seen and is prone to abuse through transitive includes that pull in tens of thousands of lines, causing slow builds that are hard to attribute to any one file.
C++ language defaults are not ideal for maintenance, so teams have to go beyond them to keep a system nimble and easy to change.

To get a heavily include-dependent C++ class into a harness, put the test in the same directory and add includes one at a time, deciding whether each dependency is really needed, rather than copying over all the include directives.
Do not just include everything until the build passes, because a long transitive-dependency chain pulls in far more than you need and may drag in things that are hard to work with under test.

Break an unwanted C++ dependency by providing an alternative empty definition for the offending method in the test file, which needs a separate build because there can be only one definition per method, and share such fakes through a common include file.

Reserve the alternative-definition C++ technique for a very huge class with severe dependency problems, because it does not break dependencies at the language level or clean the code and its duplicate definitions must be maintained; it is useful as a temporary testing point for a class you will split into smaller classes over time.

An onion parameter is when creating an object requires creating objects to create objects; the one saving grace is that at least one class must require no other class's objects, or the system could never have compiled.

Handle an onion parameter by asking what the tests really need from the parameters: Pass Null if nothing is needed, or Extract Interface or Extract Implementer on the most immediate dependency to create a fake with just the rudimentary behavior required.
In any language where you can create interfaces, or classes that act like interfaces such as C++ pure-virtual classes, you can systematically use them to break dependencies.
Extracting interfaces to break every parameter dependency clutters the design as you approach a one-to-one class-to-interface relationship, so explore other options before going there.

Ask why a parameter dependency is bad, whether creation pain, a bad side effect like touching a file or database, or slow code, because Extract Interface brutally severs the entire class, whereas if only pieces are problematic you can sever only the connection to those pieces.

Subclass and Override Method breaks a parameter dependency by overriding the problematic method, such as a validate method that hits the database, in a fake subclass to control its effect during the test.
Creating anonymous classes on the fly inside a test method is convenient for making special-case fakes, even though it is not something to do often in production code.
Subclass and Override Method needs the unwanted dependency isolated in its own method; when the dependency is intermingled with logic you need, extract methods first.

Instantiating a class is only the first part; the second is writing tests for the methods you need to change, sometimes without instantiating the class: use Expose Static Method when the method uses little instance data, or Break Out Method Object when the method is long and difficult.

The four common problems running a method in a test harness are: the method is not accessible such as being private, its parameters are hard to construct, it has bad side effects such as modifying a database, or you need to sense through an object it uses.
To change a private method, first ask whether you can test it through a public method, because doing so tests the method as it is actually used and keeps you from over-generalizing it.
Each method only needs to be functional enough to support its actual callers and clear enough to understand and change, so do not make a private method overly general just to test it.
If a private method must become public later, the first user outside the class should write test cases that explain exactly what the method does and how a caller can use it correctly.
If you need to test a private method directly, make it public; if making it public bothers you, that usually means the class is doing too much and ought to be fixed.

Two reasons making a private method public bothers us: it is a mere utility clients would not care about (minor; consider moving it to another class), or clients calling it could adversely affect other methods' results (more serious; move those methods to a new class held internally).
Good design is testable, and a design that is not testable is bad.

When you cannot afford full refactoring now, change a private method to protected and subclass to reach it in tests; this violates encapsulation slightly, but getting the tests in place is a fair trade.

Using reflection or special permissions to access private variables in tests is a cheat: do not keep such tests around, because the subterfuge hides how bad the code is getting and merely delays dealing with root causes like overly responsible classes and tangled dependencies.

Non-subclassable library classes marked sealed or final, with no public constructor, block Extract Interface and Extract Implementer, so when the class is outside your control use Adapt Parameter instead.
condition: when the parameter's class is a sealed or final library class you cannot change

statement: Adapt Parameter can subclass an unsealed superclass or abstract base that the awkward parameter type derives from and pass an object of that subclass, leaning on the compiler to make the change safe.

Skin and Wrap the API extracts an interface and writes a wrapper around an unmodifiable library class, plus a fake implementing the same interface, so your code depends on the interface rather than the concrete library class.

Depending directly on libraries that are out of your control is asking for trouble, so use sealed and final sparingly and isolate the library classes you must use behind a wrapper to gain wiggle room for changes.
Testing is straightforward only when an object does not communicate with other objects, and such objects are rare because programs build on themselves.

An undetectable side effect is when a method does its work by calling other objects, often returning no value, so the caller never learns how things turned out and there is no place to sense the result.
To test a class tangled with the GUI, first separate the GUI-independent work from the GUI-dependent work through a series of Extract Method refactorings.
When extracting methods, name them by what the code does or calculates for the class, and avoid names that reveal the display or GUI components used inside.

Command/Query Separation, from Bertrand Meyer, says a method should be a command or a query but not both: a command modifies the object's state and returns no value, and a query returns a value and does not modify the object.
Command/Query Separation matters most for communication: if a method is a query, you should not have to read its body to know you can call it several times in a row without a side effect.
After extracting the GUI-dependent methods, use Subclass and Override Method to override them in a testing subclass and test the remaining business logic.
A crude first refactoring is acceptable: coarse, even ugly, extractions are a decent first step to make a business-logic method testable, and you can clean the code up afterward.

The most hazardous part of tool-assisted refactoring is the manual editing between safe automated refactorings, and it is acceptable to extract methods with poor names or structure to get tests in place, cleaning up only after the tests exist.

Every functional change has an associated chain of effects that can propagate to callers all the way to a system boundary, while code that does not call the changed method directly or indirectly keeps its behavior.
To decide where to write tests, reason about effects: think about the change, what it affects, what those affected things affect, and so on.
Effect reasoning is a learnable skill done, for now, without tool support, and domain knowledge does not matter when reasoning about effects.

Write characterization tests to pin down existing behavior before changing it; the simplest approach is a test for each method you change, but in tangled legacy code a change in one place can affect behavior elsewhere, so that may not be enough.
When an object holds a collection by reference, such as one passed to its constructor, callers can add, replace, or mutate the collection's contents afterward and change that object's method results.
Immutable objects such as Java Strings cannot change after creation, so a getter that returns one always returns the same value and needs no effect tracing.

An effect sketch is an informal diagram with a bubble for each variable that can be affected and each method whose return value can change, and arrows to everything whose runtime value can change because of them.

Well-structured code has simple effect structures; a measure of software goodness is that complicated external effects are the sum of a much simpler set of effects in the code, and anything that simplifies the effect sketch makes code more understandable and maintainable.

Reasoning backward from a bad result to its source is debugging, whereas legacy-code work often requires reasoning forward from a point of change: if we make this change, how could it affect the rest of the program?
Writing characterization tests inverts effect analysis: you look at a set of objects and figure out what will change downstream if they stop working.
The tests you need are a description of how you expect to use the object, so you can often write them without reading the code because you already know what the object is supposed to do.
To find where to test, identify the change points, then sketch effects outward until you find the methods through which users can sense those effects, and write tests there.
When sketching effects, make sure you have found all clients of the class, including those reachable through superclasses and subclasses that can access non-private data.
Effects propagate in three basic ways: return values used by a caller, modification of objects passed as parameters and used later, and modification of static or global data used later.

Many languages pass object references by value, as Java and C# do, so any method can change the state of objects through the handle it was passed, while some languages such as C++ can forbid this with const.
The sneakiest way code can affect other code is through global or static data, because method signatures do not reveal it; information hiding is great except when it hides information you need.

The effect-reasoning heuristic is: identify the changing method; if it returns a value, check callers; if it modifies values, follow the methods that use those values transitively; check super- and subclasses that use the same variables or methods; check parameters and returned objects used by your target; and check globals or static data modified in the methods identified.

The most important tool for effect reasoning is knowledge of your language, because every language has firewalls that stop effect propagation, and knowing them means you do not have to look past them.

Know your language's subtleties: in C++ a const method cannot modify instance variables, but a mutable member can still be changed in a const method, so taking const at face value without checking is dangerous.

Field visibility changes the effect scope: private fields limit effects to the class's own methods, whereas package-scoped or protected fields let package clients or subclasses access them directly, so those must be checked.
Basic goodness in a code base is a set of often-implicit rules that let you rule out effects you would otherwise have to check, whereas in bad code the rules are unknown or riddled with exceptions.

Programming gets easier as you narrow effects, because you need to know less to understand a piece of code, and restricting effects in object-oriented code makes testing much easier with no real hurdles.

Removing tiny pieces of duplication, such as having one method call another internally instead of repeating its logic, yields effect sketches with fewer endpoints, which often makes testing decisions easier.

Many dependency-breaking techniques break encapsulation, and encapsulation matters because it helps you reason about code by leaving fewer paths to follow, but it is a tool for understanding, not an end in itself.
When encapsulation and test coverage conflict, bias toward test coverage, because good explanatory tests let you reason about the code directly and often help you get more encapsulation later.

Test one level back: write tests at a single public method for changes in several private methods, or at one object's interface for a collaboration of objects it holds, to cover several changes at once and give yourself cover for further refactoring.

Higher-level covering tests are a useful first step toward unit tests, not a substitute for them, and changing them is often easier than feared because you change the tests and then the code in small, safe increments.
An interception point is a point in the program where you can detect the effects of a change; find them by tracing effects outward from your change points, using judgment about which is best.

Pick interception points as close to your change points as possible, because fewer steps between the change and the interception point make a stronger safety argument and usually make the test easier to set up.
The best interception point is usually a public method on the class being changed, which is easy to find and use, though it is not always the best choice.

When changing a cluster of classes, a higher-level interception point can be more efficient: it means less dependency breaking and holds a bigger chunk in the vise, giving more cover to refactor the internals while the higher-level tests stay invariant.
A pinch point is a narrowing in an effect sketch, a place where tests against one or two methods can detect changes in many methods.
Pinch points are determined by the change points, not just by a class's clients, so a class with multiple clients can still have a good pinch point for a given set of changes.

If you cannot find a single pinch point, revisit your change points because you may be doing too much at once; find pinch points for one or two changes at a time, or else write tests for individual changes as close as you can.

Find a pinch point by looking for common usage across an effect sketch: a method with several users may be used the same way, so testing in one place can suffice, gated by asking whether breaking the method would be sensed there.

A pinch point is a natural encapsulation boundary, a narrow funnel for all the effects of a large piece of code, and noticing pinch points reveals how to reallocate responsibilities across classes for better encapsulation.
Use effect sketches to find hidden classes: a group of methods and fields that form a natural encapsulation boundary within a large class can be extracted into its own class.

To find hidden classes, ignore the bubble names in an effect sketch and look only at how they group into natural encapsulation boundaries, then name each cluster, since that name can become a new class.
Do naming and extraction discussions with teammates, because they build a shared view of what the system is and can become, with benefits beyond the current work.
Pinch-point tests are temporary scaffolding: after carving out and characterizing a cluster, write narrower per-class unit tests and eventually delete the pinch-point tests.
Do not let unit tests grow into mini-integration tests by instantiating many collaborators, because such tests become big, bulky, and slow to run.

When writing unit tests for new code, test classes as independently as possible; if tests get too large, break the class into smaller independent pieces and fake collaborators, because a unit test's job is one object's behavior, not a cluster's.

Finding bugs in legacy code is usually not the hard part and can be misdirected effort; the winning strategy is to help the team write correct code consistently and avoid putting bugs in in the first place.

Automated tests are not directly for bug finding: they should specify a goal to fulfill or preserve behavior that already exists, and in the natural flow of development tests that specify become tests that preserve, catching bugs in later runs when behavior changes unexpectedly.

In legacy code without tests, bolster the area you are about to change with tests as a safety net; you will find bugs along the way, but making find-and-fix-all-bugs the goal means you will never finish.
A characterization test characterizes the actual current behavior of a piece of code, documenting what the system really does rather than what it should do.

The characterization-test algorithm is: use the code in a test harness, write an assertion you know will fail, let the failure reveal the actual behavior, change the test to expect that behavior, and repeat.

Characterization tests have no moral authority: they document what the code does rather than a gold standard, so if a characterized value looks like a bug, keep the test but mark it suspicious and investigate the effect of fixing it.

Characterization is not black-box testing: you may read the code you are characterizing; get curious and write tests until you understand it, then add tests until you are confident they will sense the problems your intended change could cause, and if you cannot reach that confidence, change the software a different way.

The Method Use Rule: before using a method in a legacy system, check whether tests exist for it and write them if not, so tests become a medium of communication and making the class testable itself tends to increase code quality.

Heuristics for characterizing a class: use a sensing variable for tangled logic, list what can go wrong for each responsibility and test it, test extreme input values, and write tests for invariants that should hold throughout the object's lifetime, refactoring to discover them.

Write characterization tests as documentation for a reader: order them from easy cases that show the class's main intent to cases that highlight its idiosyncrasies, and record the important things you discover.

When you find a bug while characterizing: if the system was never deployed, fix it; if it was deployed, someone may depend on the behavior, so analyze how to fix without ripple effects; bias toward fixing clear errors promptly, and mark suspected ones suspicious and escalate.
Targeted testing: after writing tests to understand a section of code, verify that your tests actually cover the specific thing you are going to change.

When you write a test for a branch, ask whether the test could pass any way other than by executing that branch, and if you are unsure, use a sensing variable or the debugger to confirm the branch is hit.
Watch for inputs whose special behavior could make a test pass when it should fail, and pick inputs that force an error such as a double-to-int truncation to be visible.
When refactoring, check two things: that the behavior still exists after the refactoring and that it is connected correctly.
Many characterization tests are sunny-day tests that just verify a behavior is present, from which you can infer that a move or extract refactoring preserved behavior.
The most valuable characterization tests exercise a specific path and exercise each conversion along that path.

To catch conversion or truncation errors, manually compute expected values checking each conversion, step through with a debugger, use sensing variables to confirm the path and conversions run, or characterize a smaller chunk of code.
Refactoring tools have quirks, such as extracting an expression as add(y) instead of add(x,y) because x is an instance variable, so even with a tool you sometimes have to refactor by hand.

Heuristic for characterization tests: write tests for the area you will change until you understand it, then write tests for the specific things you will change, and if you are extracting or moving functionality, verify each behavior's existence and connection case by case and exercise the conversions.

Library reuse saves time but it is easy to become over-reliant, and promiscuous direct use locks you in, so that a vendor royalty hike can make an application unsellable and switching vendors can amount to a rewrite.
Avoid littering direct calls to library classes throughout your code, because the belief that you will never change them can become a self-fulfilling prophecy.
Every hard-coded use of a library class is a place where you could have had a seam.
When a library class is final or sealed or has non-virtual key functions with no way to fake it under test, write a thin wrapper over the classes you need to separate out.
condition: when the library class cannot be faked because it is final, sealed, or non-virtual

statement: Library designers who use language features to enforce design constraints often make a mistake, because good code runs in both production and test environments and constraints aimed at production can make working in test nearly impossible.
The once dilemma is that a library assuming a single instance of a class makes fake objects hard to introduce, so sometimes wrapping the singleton is the only choice.

The restricted override dilemma is that non-virtual methods hinder sensing and separation; you can pretend a public method is non-virtual in production code and override it selectively in test to get the best of both worlds.
A coding convention can be just as good as a restrictive language feature, so think about what your tests need.
To restructure an API-heavy application, first identify its computational core by writing a brief description of what the code really does for you.

Separate an API-heavy program into responsibilities, noting which are tied to the API and which are not, because even a small factoring into classes and interfaces gives layering and gets the core logic under test.

Nearly every system has some core logic that can be peeled away from API calls, and it is nearly impossible to break a system into smaller pieces without ending up with some that are higher level than others.

When a system looks like nothing but API calls, imagine it as one big object and apply responsibility-separation heuristics, because just identifying the responsibilities makes better decisions easier even before you can improve the design.

Skin and Wrap the API makes interfaces mirroring the API and wrappers around library classes while preserving signatures, so you can end up with no dependency on the underlying API, with wrappers delegating to the real API in production and to fakes in test.

Responsibility-Based Extraction identifies responsibilities in the code and extracts methods for them, and it needs a tool that provides safe extract-method support or confidence to do the extractions by hand.

Choose Skin and Wrap the API when the API is small, you want to fully separate a third-party dependency, or you have no tests and cannot test through the API, and choose Responsibility-Based Extraction when the API is more complicated and you can extract methods safely.

Skin and Wrap gets everything under test except a thin delegation layer but is more work, while Responsibility-Based Extraction may pull your own logic in with API code and leave the extracted code untestable but lets code depend on higher-level interfaces; many teams use both, a thin wrapper for testing plus a higher-level wrapper for a better interface.
When reading code gets confusing, draw pictures and make notes; the sketches need not be formal UML, and sketching helps you see things differently and maintain your mental state on complex code.
Sketching is informal and infectious, so you can spread it on a team simply by sketching while you explain code to an engaged partner, without mandating it as process.

Listing markup means printing the code and marking it according to your goal: group related things to separate responsibilities, line up blocks to understand structure, circle extractable code, or mark changed and affected lines to understand effects.
Line up blocks in a long method inside-out by matching each closing brace to its opening brace, working from the first closing brace outward, to make deeply indented code readable.
Scratch refactoring: check the code out, refactor it freely to understand it without writing tests, then throw it away without checking it in; it is one of the best ways to learn how code works.

Scratch refactoring has two risks: a gross refactoring mistake can give you a false view of the system, and becoming too attached to the scratch result can make you miss better structures and insights when you really refactor.
Delete code you can confirm is unused, because it only gets in your way, and version control preserves it if you ever need it again, so deleting it is not wasteful.
Long-lived applications tend to sprawl: under schedule pressure they degrade until nobody understands the complete structure, and people add features at the hack points they know best.
When a team is not aware of its architecture it degrades, and awareness is blocked when the system is too complex to grasp, has no big picture, or the team is in constant reactive emergency mode.
An architect must work with the team day to day, or the code diverges from the big picture, either because someone does something inappropriate or because the big picture itself needs to change.
Architecture is too important to be left to a few people: keep it intact by ensuring everyone who touches the code knows it and has a stake in it, which amplifies the team's overall intelligence.

Telling the Story of the System: one person asks another to explain the architecture using only a few concepts, pretending the listener knows nothing, then adds the next most important thing each round until the core design is covered.

Telling the story forces you to simplify and abstract, which can feel like lying by omission, but articulating the simple ideal view shows what would be ideal versus what exists as expediency and forces you to identify what is important.

Use the story of the system as a design guide: prefer changes that fall in line with the story and make it feel less of a lie, and when choosing between two implementations, pick the one that leads to an easier-to-understand system.

Adding a responsibility that the simplest story of the system never mentions is a bolder distortion than generalizing the story slightly, so prefer changes that keep the core story substantially true.

As systems grow they inevitably get more complicated, and a system being more complex than its simplest story does not make it bad, because the story gives guidance rather than a standard the system must meet.
Tell the story of the system often and in different ways on a team to share a common view and get your bearings for where to add features.

Naked CRC describes a system by laying down and moving blank index cards to convey the typical objects and their interactions, using motion and position to make involved scenarios graspable and memorable.
Naked CRC has two guidelines: cards represent instances rather than classes, and overlapping cards shows a collection of them.

Listen to conversations about your design: when a concept recurs in conversation, such as a locking policy, create a class for it with method names that describe the intent instead of writing the logic inline.

Compare the concepts used in conversation with the concepts in the code; a weak overlap signals that either the code has not adapted to the team's understanding or the team needs to understand it differently, so put that understanding into the code.

Design is design regardless of when in the development cycle it happens, and one of the worst mistakes is feeling design is over while changes continue, because new code then lands in poor places and classes bloat since no one dares introduce abstraction.

Establish naming conventions so test code does not swamp you: use a Test suffix so each test class lists next to its class, a Fake prefix for fake collaborators, and a Testing prefix for testing subclasses.
Ergonomics matters: arrange classes so it is easy to navigate back and forth between a class and its tests.

Decide test location by deployment size constraints: if space is not a concern, keep tests and production code in the same directories, but if the software ships on someone else's machine, deployment size may force separation.
If navigating up and down directories between code and its tests is painful, people stop writing tests and work slows, like paying a tax as you work.
An alternative to separate directories is to keep code and tests together and use scripts or build settings, aided by good naming conventions, to strip the test code from the deployment.

If you separate test and production code, do it for a good reason rather than mere aesthetics, because later navigation becomes painful and you can get used to tests sitting next to production source.

Procedural languages are especially challenging for legacy work because they lack the seams that object-oriented and many functional languages have, though careful dependency management can compensate.

Because breaking dependencies in procedural code is hard, the best strategy is often to get a large chunk under test first by finding a pinch point and using a link seam, or a preprocessing seam if the language has a macro preprocessor, and then use those tests for feedback.

Link-seam faking in C, with a fake library of same-named functions, works when the faked functions are peripheral, but is tedious for sensing or varying return values because link-time substitution allows only one definition per executable.
C's macro preprocessor can define an unwanted call out of existence under a TESTING flag and add test stubs, and keeping the tests in a separate included file keeps the production code readable.
Restrict rampant macro usage to code that runs under test, so you do not risk misusing macros in ways that affect production code.
In procedural legacy code, bias toward introducing new functions rather than adding code to existing ones, because at least you can write tests for the new functions.
Test-driven development works in both object-oriented and procedural code, and formulating a test for each piece of code you are about to write often leads you to alter its design in good ways.

Reformulate procedural code to separate pure logic from dependencies: put the computational logic in its own testable function and leave a thin wrapper function that binds the logic to the dependency.

For functions dominated by external calls where sequencing matters and there is little computation, you may skip writing the test first and test at a higher level; in C, a struct of function pointers gives a seam, pointing to real functions in production and fakes in test.

Object seams have nice properties: they are easy to notice in the code, they help break code into smaller understandable pieces, and seams introduced for testing can be useful later when you extend the software.

When a procedural language offers an object-oriented migration path, use it: for example compile C as C++, then Encapsulate Global References by wrapping the offending free function in a class while preserving signatures, route calls through a global instance, and apply Parameterize Constructor to inject a test double.
Mechanical dependency-breaking migration changes are not great object-oriented design but are good enough to use as a wedge to break dependencies and enable testing going forward.

Every procedural program is effectively object-oriented but often contains only one big object, and Encapsulate Global References subdivides that one object into new objects that are easier to work with.

When a procedural language has object-oriented extensions, use them to move incrementally toward a better object design by grouping related functions into classes and extracting methods to break apart tangled responsibilities.
Object seams do far more than get tests in place, whereas link and preprocessing seams get code under test but do little to improve design beyond that.
Continually adding little tweaks to existing classes leads to long methods and large classes, turning the software into a swamp where understanding and adding features takes more time.

Big classes cause three problems: confusion about what to change and what it affects, task-scheduling thrashing because many reasons to change make concurrent programmers collide, and being a pain to test.

Over-encapsulation is harmful: when a class hides too much, its internals rot with no easy way to sense the effects of change, forcing people back to Edit-and-Pray programming with slow changes or more bugs.

To avoid making a big class worse while changing it, use Sprout Class and Sprout Method to put new code in a new class or method rather than growing the existing one, and the new method's name also hints at how to break the class down.
The key remedy for big classes is refactoring them into sets of smaller classes, and the biggest challenge is figuring out what the smaller classes should be.
The Single Responsibility Principle states that every class should have a single responsibility, a single purpose in the system and only one reason to change.
In real big-class cases, identify the different responsibilities and incrementally move toward more focused ones, rather than designing a hypothetical multiclass ideal you will not actually build.
Discovering responsibilities in existing code is the same design skill as formulating them for new code, and you are not inventing responsibilities but discovering what is already there.

Heuristic Group Methods: list all methods with their access types and find ones that go together; you need not categorize all of them, and finding a responsibility off to the side of the main one gives a direction, extracting the class when you next modify one of those methods.
Method grouping is a good team exercise, for example putting poster boards of each major class's method names in the team room and marking up groupings over time.

Heuristic Hidden Methods: many private or protected methods often indicate another class dying to get out, and the urge to test a private method means it should be public, which, if it bothers you, means it belongs on another class.
Moving methods to a new class where they become public does not reduce the original class's encapsulation, because the original still accesses them privately through that new class.

Heuristic Decisions That Can Change: look for already-made decisions that seem hard-coded, such as a specific database or API, and extract methods named for your high-level intent, which encapsulates the resource and breaks dependencies on low-level details.
Method names do not tell the whole story, because a big class's methods often do many things at many abstraction levels, so do some extract-method refactoring before settling on classes to extract.

Heuristic Internal Relationships: look for instance variables used by some methods and not others, and draw a feature sketch mapping which variables and methods each method uses to reveal clusters within the class.

Feature sketches and effect sketches have the same shape with reversed arrows: feature sketches point to what a method uses to map internal structure, and effect sketches point to what is impacted to reason forward from a change; both are disposable ten-minute tools.
Circle groups of features in a sketch to explore a split: the lines you cross define the new class's interface, and naming each group builds naming skill and explores design alternatives.
A pinch point inside a class shows up as a small set of lines connecting larger feature clusters and marks a natural place to split, though pinch points are not always present.

Heuristic Primary Responsibility: describe the class's responsibility in a single sentence, adding a clause per client need, and if one thing seems more important than the rest it is the key responsibility while the others should be factored out.

The Single Responsibility Principle can be violated at the interface level, where the interface makes the class look responsible for many things, or at the implementation level, where the class actually does all of it rather than delegating; the implementation-level violation matters most.
Fix an interface-level Single Responsibility violation with client-specific interfaces, creating an interface per client grouping so each client sees the big class through only its own interface.

The Interface Segregation Principle observes that rarely do all a large class's clients use all its methods, so per-client interfaces hide information, decrease dependency, and stop clients recompiling when the big class changes, after which you can move code out to a new class that uses the original.

Segregating an interface is harder than it sounds, often requiring you to expose more of the original class and change client code, which needs tests around those clients first, but it lets you whittle down the big class's interface.

When you cannot otherwise see the responsibilities in a class, do some scratch refactoring, remembering it is an artificial exercise and the things you see are not necessarily what you will end up with.

Focus on Current Work: the change you are making right now reveals a particular way the software can change, and recognizing that way is often enough to see your new code as a separate responsibility to extract and allow substitution for.
Do not be overwhelmed by all the responsibilities you can identify in a class; let the change you are currently making guide which responsibility you extract.

The real way to get better at identifying responsibilities is to read more: design-pattern books and, more importantly, other people's code, paying attention to naming and the correspondence between class and method names.

Avoid large refactoring binges, because teams that go on them see system stability break down for a while even when careful and writing tests; a binge is only advisable early in the release cycle with time and accepted risk.
