The best approach to breaking down big classes is to identify the responsibilities, make sure the team understands them, and then break the class down on an as-needed basis, which spreads out the risk of the changes.

Start by applying the Single Responsibility Principle at the implementation level, extracting classes and delegating to them, because interface-level SRP requires changing clients and having tests for them, and doing implementation-level first makes interface-level easier later.

Before extracting a class, list the instance variables and methods you will move to know what to write tests for, and cover private methods you plan to move by testing through the public methods that use them.
If you can get tests in place, extract a class with the Extract Class refactoring, and if you cannot, you can still extract classes conservatively through a mechanical, tool-independent procedure.

The conservative extract-class-without-tests procedure is: identify the responsibility, move its instance variables to a separate part of the declaration, extract each method's body into a new method with a MOVING prefix while preserving signatures, text-search the class and subclasses to ensure moved variables are not used outside the moved methods, then move everything to the new class and lean on the compiler, and finally remove the MOVING prefix.

Do not lean on the compiler to find uses of a variable that might be shadowed, because a subclass can declare a same-named variable, so commenting out the declaration only exposes the shadowed one and the compiler will not find all uses; search manually instead.

Extracting classes without tests risks inheritance bugs: moving a method that overrides another makes callers hit the base-class method, and moving a variable that hides a superclass variable exposes the hidden one, so extract new methods from the old bodies rather than moving the originals.

After extracting a class, the biggest danger is getting overambitious, because the existing structure works and supports the functionality, so sometimes formulate the ideal view, forget it, and move the code in a better direction rather than all the way to the ideal.
Removing duplication does not require a grand re-engineering effort; you can do it in small chunks as you work, and the system gets better over time as long as people do not reintroduce duplication.
Whether zealously removing duplication in an area helps can be hard to tell just by looking, so try removing it, see where you end up, and then decide.
Before refactoring to remove duplication, have a set of tests that you run after each refactoring step.
Remove small pieces of duplication first, because over-thinking the end structure wastes time and small removals make larger areas of duplication easier to see.

When a series of duplication removals could yield different structures depending on where you start, it does not matter much structurally since you can refactor between them, so decide by which grouping yields a better name.
When two methods look roughly the same, extract the differences into other methods, which can make the two methods exactly the same so you can delete one.
To pull a shared method up to a superclass when subclasses differ only in data, introduce an abstract getter or abstract hook method that the subclasses override, then move the common method up.

Generalize remaining duplication by data, for example replacing per-field code with a list of fields that each subclass constructor populates, so a single loop in the superclass handles computing body size and writing.
Removing duplication across classes leaves you with very small focused methods, each doing something no other method does, which gives orthogonality.
Orthogonality means independence: if there is exactly one place to change a given behavior, changes are easy, whereas rampant duplication gives you more than one knob per behavior.
When behavior is localized in single methods it is easy to replace or add to it, for example overriding a writeField or writeBody method for special cases.

Removing duplication is largely mechanical, moving methods and variables and breaking down methods, and the only creative part is naming, so you are moving code closer to its essence rather than designing from scratch.
Designs emerge when you remove duplication zealously, because most of the knobs you need in the application just happen rather than being planned.
Duplication removal is a powerful way to distill a design: it makes the design more flexible and makes change faster and easier.
Abbreviations in class and method names are problematic: they can be acceptable when used consistently, but inconsistent abbreviation forces you to look names up and guess wrong.
Use names consistently, because you are less likely to be wrong when class and method names follow a consistent convention.

Extract shared behavior into a superclass but do not over-collapse the hierarchy: even when subclasses become thin, keeping them can be better than static methods that would force all client code to change.
The Open/Closed Principle, from Bertrand Meyer, says code should be open for extension but closed to modification, meaning with good design you do not have to change much code to add new features.
Removing duplication makes code naturally fall in line with the Open/Closed Principle.
Long methods are quagmires that you must re-understand on each change; you can sometimes avoid refactoring them with Sprout Method and Sprout Class, but they still cost time.
A monster method is a method so long and complex, often hundreds or thousands of lines, that you do not feel comfortable touching it.

Monster methods come in two varieties: bulleted methods with little indentation that read as a sequence of code chunks, and snarled methods dominated by a single large indented and nested section, with most real methods a mix of the two.
Bulleted methods resist naive extract-a-method-per-section because temporaries declared in one section are used in the next, though their lack of wild indentation keeps you oriented.
To tell whether you have a real snarl, try to line up the blocks in the method; if you feel vertigo, it is a snarled method.

A refactoring tool makes a big difference on long methods: safe extract-method support means you do not need tests to verify your extractions, whereas without it cleanup is bounded by the tests you can get in place.
Refactoring tools do not perform auxiliary refactorings such as reordering statements, and no current tool checks whether reordering is safe, which makes manual reordering a source of bugs.

To use a refactoring tool effectively on large methods, make a series of changes solely with the tool and avoid all other edits, even reordering statements or breaking apart expressions, which cleanly separates known-safe changes from unverified ones; get tests in place afterward to verify any manual edits.

When breaking up a monster method, the key goals of your extractions are to separate logic from awkward dependencies and to introduce seams that make it easier to get tests in place for more refactoring.

When extracting with a tool, do coarse work safely and handle the details after getting other tests in place, and do not worry about extracted methods that do not fit the class because they often point toward a new class to extract later.

Extracted-method names that seem hokey are still a good starting point, because they let the code communicate at a higher level and introduce seams for breaking dependencies, and you can rename them later as they settle into place.
Without a refactoring tool, correctness is your responsibility and tests are the strongest tool available, while monster methods make testing, refactoring, and feature addition very difficult.

Common extract-method errors without tests are: forgetting to pass a variable in, which can be masked when it shares an instance variable's name; naming the extracted method so it hides or overrides a base-class method; and mistakes passing parameters or assigning and returning wrong values or types.

Introduce Sensing Variable: temporarily add a variable to sense a condition inside the method you are refactoring, engineer input to cover it, extract that logic, then remove the variable and its tests when done.
Keep sensing variables in the class across a series of refactorings and delete them only after the session, so you can see and easily undo the extraction tests.
Sensing variables are a key tool for teasing apart monster methods and for progressively de-snarling deeply nested code by extracting conditionals and their bodies.
Extract What You Know: start small by finding two-to-five-line chunks you can name and extract confidently without tests, then add tests to cover them.

Coupling count is the number of values passing into and out of an extracted method; favor low-count extractions because mistakes are less likely, and accesses of instance variables do not count because they are copied out rather than passed through the method's interface.

The key danger in method extraction is a type-conversion error, which you avoid by extracting low-coupling-count methods and checking where each passed variable is declared to get the signature right.

Zero-count extractions with no parameters and no return value are the safest of all; they are commands to act on state, and naming them often yields insight that cascades into new design perspectives.
With Extract What You Know, do not choose chunks that are too large, use a sensing variable when the coupling count is greater than zero, and write a few tests for the method after extracting.
Extracting zero-count methods is a good way to get a sense of a monster method's overall structure when you have no refactoring tool, and it is a good prelude to testing and further work.

Gleaning Dependencies: write tests for the critical behavior you must preserve, then extract the things the tests do not cover, so you preserve the important behavior even while editing uncovered code.
Not all behaviors in an application are equal; some are more critical, and Gleaning Dependencies is particularly powerful when critical behavior is tangled with other behavior.

Break Out Method Object: create a class whose only responsibility is the monster method's work, turning the method's parameters into constructor parameters and its body into a run or execute method, then convert the local variables into instance variables to sense through as you break the method down.
Break Out Method Object uses variables that are needed for production, unlike a sensing variable, so it lets you build up tests that you keep.

Skeletonize Methods: extract a conditional's test and body into separate methods so only the control structure and delegations remain, which is better when the control structure will need to be refactored after it is clarified.

Find Sequences: extract a conditional's test and body together into one method, which better positions you to identify a common overarching sequence of operations, and is better when seeing that sequence makes the code clearer.
Bulleted methods lean toward finding sequences and snarled methods toward skeletonizing, but the choice really depends on the design insight you get while doing the extractions.

Extract to the current class first even when a chunk clearly belongs on another class, using the awkward name, because it is easily undoable and less error-prone, and you can move the method to the other class later when the best direction presents itself.
If the name you are tempted to use for an extracted chunk is one of the variables it uses, that code probably belongs on that variable's class.

Extract small pieces first: each seems to make no difference, but after several extractions you see the method differently, such as a hidden sequence or a better organization, which is far safer than breaking it into large chunks from the start where the details that make the code work are easily missed.

Be prepared to redo extractions: after some extractions you often find a better structure, and undoing and re-extracting is not wasted effort because the first attempt gave you insight into the old design and a better path forward.

Code does not fatigue like physical materials: left alone it never breaks, and the only way it gains a fault is someone editing it, which makes developers the primary agents that introduce faults and makes it very easy to do so.

Hyperaware editing means knowing exactly what each keystroke does, since every keystroke either changes behavior or does not, and fast sub-second test runs with test-driven development tighten that feedback loop and reduce bugs.

Distinguish refactoring keystrokes from functional-change keystrokes, because changing a numeric literal in used code is a functional change rather than a refactoring, and knowing which you are doing as you type matters.

Tests and pair programming foster hyperaware editing, a refreshing flow state, whereas editing without feedback is the exhausting and scary state of holding all the changed and unchanged state in your head.

Judgment is a key programming skill, and trying to act like a super-smart programmer who holds the whole system in their head gets you into trouble, because holding lots of mental state does not improve decision-making.

Single-Goal Editing: programming is the art of doing one thing at a time, so if you are doing more than one thing, pick one and write the other down for later, because doing one thing deliberately is faster than thrashing across multiple pending changes.

Refactoring is particularly error-prone because it involves invasive editing at a larger scale than adding a line, and while the general defense is tests, the initial dependency-breaking refactorings must be done without tests and so must be particularly conservative.
Do not do extra cleanup while breaking dependencies without tests, because combining a mechanical extraction with design improvement introduces mistakes that are found far later than they need to be.

Preserve Signatures: avoid changing signatures so you can cut, copy, and paste entire argument lists verbatim to minimize errors, which makes the moves automatic and frees attention for other error sources such as hiding a base-class method.

Lean on the Compiler: in a statically typed language, deliberately alter a declaration to cause compile errors, then navigate to each error and make the change, letting the compiler do the legwork for structural or type changes such as switching a variable's type from a class to an interface.
Know exactly what the compiler will and will not find when you lean on it, so you are not lulled into false confidence, because leaning blindly can introduce subtle bugs.

Inheritance is the biggest source of error when leaning on the compiler: commenting out a method or variable that also exists concretely in a superclass produces no error but silently switches to the superclass version, so no error does not mean the member is unused.
Leaning on the compiler is not always practical, because if builds take a long time it may be more practical to search for the places where you need to make changes instead.
condition: when builds are slow

statement: Pair programming increases quality and spreads knowledge, and you should pair when using dependency-breaking techniques, because it is easy to break software unknowingly and legacy work is surgery, where doctors never operate alone.

The grass is not greener in green-field development: the effort to replace a legacy system routinely fails because the old system keeps changing under the new team, and the maintainers turn out to be tending the critical investment everyone will rely on.

The attitude a team brings to legacy work matters, since teams with millions of lines of legacy code can treat each day as a chance to improve and have fun while teams with better code bases can be dejected.

To lift low morale that comes from poor code quality, pick the ugliest, most obnoxious set of classes and get them under test as a team, because tackling the worst problem makes you feel in control of the situation.

Dependency-breaking techniques are behavior-preserving refactorings that, unlike most, are intended to be done without tests to get tests in place; following the steps carefully keeps mistakes small, but you should still exercise care.

Dependency-breaking techniques do not immediately make the design better, and some will make you flinch, but they get code under test so the system is more maintainable, after which test-supported refactorings can clean the design.

Use Adapt Parameter to break a parameter dependency when you cannot Extract Interface on the parameter's class, such as a standard library interface you cannot modify, or when the parameter is difficult to fake.
condition: when Extract Interface is not possible on the parameter's class

statement: Extract Interface is often the best choice for breaking parameter dependencies, but it is counterproductive or impossible when the parameter's type is low-level or specific to some implementation technology.

Adapt Parameter wraps the incoming parameter behind a new narrow interface you define that returns just what you need, with a production implementer wrapping the real API and a fake for tests, decoupling your logic from the specific API.
Move toward interfaces that communicate responsibilities rather than implementation details, because this makes code easier to read and easier to maintain.

A pervasive legacy problem is the absence of abstraction layers, with the most important code intermingled with low-level API calls, and narrow abstractions targeted at what you need make the code communicate better and leave a better seam.

Adapt Parameter is one case where you do not Preserve Signatures, so use extra care; it is risky if the simplified interface differs too much from the original, and your bias should be toward changes you feel confident in rather than the best structure, which can come after tests.

The steps for Adapt Parameter are: create a simple, communicative interface for the method; create a production implementer; create a fake implementer; write a simple test passing the fake to the method; change the method to use the new parameter; and run the test to verify.
When breaking dependencies, look ahead to what the result will look like and decide whether you can live with the aftermath before choosing an approach.

Break Out Method Object moves a long method into a new method-object class whose objects embody the method's code, letting local variables become instance variables so it is easier to break dependencies and write tests.

Choose between Expose Static Method and Break Out Method Object by the method: if it is small and does not use instance data, use Expose Static Method, and if it is large or uses instance data and methods, use Break Out Method Object.

Break Out Method Object has variations: if the method uses no instance members, do not pass the original class; if it only uses the class's data, pass that data as a new data-holding class; and the worst case, using the class's methods, needs Extract Interface to build abstraction from the original class.

Getting a method object under test may force you to make private members public temporarily, but that is not the end, because over time you break dependencies to instantiate the original class and can evolve toward a better design.
Definition Completion in C or C++ declares a method in a header but provides an alternate definition in the test file to break a dependency under test.

Definition Completion requires a separate test executable to avoid link clashes and creates two definition sets that are a maintenance burden and can confuse debuggers, so reserve it for the worst dependency situations, use it only to break initial dependencies, and bring the class under test quickly to remove the duplicates.

To test code with problematic global dependencies you have three choices: make the globals act differently under test, link to different globals, or encapsulate the global references to decouple things further.
If several globals are always used or modified near each other, they belong in the same class.

Name a new class for the methods that will eventually reside on it; the name should be good but not perfect since you can rename it later, and if the name is already in use, consider renaming whatever currently uses it.

Encapsulate Global References wraps globals in a class, declares a global instance, and leans on the compiler to prefix each reference, a behavior-preserving transformation that yields uglier but separated code you can then parameterize.

When breaking dependencies without tests, leave the logic alone as much as possible and get separation by inserting seams that let you call one method or access one datum rather than another, moving behavior between classes only later once tests are in place.
When using Encapsulate Global References, start with data or small methods and move more substantial methods to the new class only when more tests are in place.
To encapsulate references to free functions, make an interface class with fake and production subclasses, where each production function does nothing more than delegate to the global function.

Prefer the class-and-virtual-function approach, then parameterize the class, over free functions delegating to free functions or static functions, because only the former gives explicit, easy-to-manage seams instead of requiring a link or preprocessing seam.
Referencing a class member instead of a global is only the first step; afterward consider Introduce Static Setter, Parameterize Constructor, or Parameterize Method to obtain the test seam.
Expose Static Method: if a method uses no instance data or methods, make it static so you can get it under test without instantiating the class.
condition: when the method uses no instance data or methods

statement: A static method that touches no private data is effectively a utility not part of the class proper, since the static area behaves like a separate metaclass, so exposing it public to test it is acceptable and the tests support you if you move it later.

The static portion of a class is a staging area for things that do not quite belong to it, so if a method uses no instance data, make it static to make it noticeable until you figure out which class it really belongs on.
If you fear an exposed static method will be misused, restrict its access with package, internal, or protected visibility accessed through a testing subclass, or a namespace in C++.

Extract and Override Call extracts a single problematic call, such as a static or global, into a local method, then overrides it in a testing subclass to break the dependency or sense the values passed to it.
Use Extract and Override Call unless there are many different calls against the same global, in which case use Replace Global Reference with Getter instead.
Hard-coded object creation and initialization work in constructors can be very hard to work around in testing.

Extract and Override Factory Method extracts a constructor's object-creation into a factory method that a testing subclass overrides to return a fake, but it does not work in C++, where a base constructor cannot call a derived virtual, so use Supersede Instance Variable or Extract and Override Getter there.

Extract and Override Getter introduces a lazy getter that creates the object on first call, routes all uses through it, then subclasses and overrides the getter to supply a fake, serving as the C++ workaround for the factory-method constructor limitation.
A lazy getter looks like a normal getter to callers but constructs the object it returns the first time it is called, and is also used in the Singleton Design Pattern.

With Extract and Override Getter, be conscious of object-lifetime issues in non-garbage-collected languages by deleting the testing instance consistently with the production instance, and make all class code use the getter to avoid using the variable before it is initialized.
Use Extract and Override Call for a single problematic method on an object, but Extract and Override Getter when there are many problematic methods on the same object.

Extract Implementer turns a class into an interface by subclassing it and pushing all its concrete methods down into a production subclass, useful when the class's name is perfect for the interface and you lack a rename or extract-interface tool.
Do not prefix interface names with I unless it is already the convention in the code base, because a mix of I-prefixed and non-prefixed type names makes you guess the name wrong about half the time.

Naming is a key part of design: good names reinforce understanding of a system and make it easier to work with, while poor names undermine understanding and make life hellish for the programmers who follow.

Extract Implementer only replaces the creation of one concrete class with another and so does not improve the overall dependency situation by itself, so examine those creation sites for whether a factory can reduce dependencies further.
When a class is embedded in an inheritance hierarchy, consider whether Extract Interface with different interface names is more direct than Extract Implementer.

Extract Interface is one of the safest dependency-breaking techniques in many languages because a wrong step is caught by the compiler immediately: create an interface with the methods you need in a context, implement it to sense or separate, and pass a fake into the class under test.

There are three ways to Extract Interface: automated tool support, which is safest and can update references; incremental manual steps; or cutting and pasting several method declarations at once, which is less safe but often the only practical way without tooling and with slow builds.

The I-prefix interface naming convention avoids naming effort but forces code to know it is dealing with an interface, mixes I-prefixed and non-prefixed names, and makes later reverting to a regular class a pervasive change or leaves the name as a subtle lie.

Prefer simple class names even for big abstractions, and if you later need an interface, subclass the class, push its data and methods down, and make the original name the interface, so you do not have to rename every reference.

When extracting an interface you do not have to extract all of a class's public methods; lean on the compiler to find the used ones, reach a full-coverage interface incrementally, and hold off on the pervasive change until you have more test coverage.

Extract Interface has a non-virtual pitfall: pulling a non-virtual method's signature into an interface makes it virtual, which changes behavior if the class has subclasses that redefine it in C++ or C#, whereas Java is safe because all instance methods are already virtual.

Creating a derived-class method with the same signature as a non-virtual base method is bad practice in C++, so to expose a non-virtual function through an interface on a class that has subclasses, add a new virtual method with a new name that delegates to it.

Utility classes of only static methods and constants are usually created when no common abstraction can be found for a set of methods, but in nearly all cases you can use plain classes with instance data and methods instead.

Static cling is when a static method depends on something hard to depend on in a test; Introduce Instance Delegator adds a delegating instance method and passes the object in, giving you an object seam to substitute behavior under test.
Once every call to a utility class comes through delegating instance methods, move the static method bodies into the instance methods and delete the static methods.
Global mutable data is often the most apparent hurdle to getting a system under test, a kind of spooky action at a distance, because you must set up each global's state before you can test.
Removing access protection to add a static setter is acceptable, because the purpose of access protection is to prevent errors and tests also prevent errors, and here you need the stronger tool.
The ultimate better state for a singleton is to reduce global references to it until it can just become a normal class.
A global factory serves fresh objects from static methods, and you make it substitutable under test by having it delegate to a swappable factory object behind an interface with a set-server method.
Static-setter patterns modify state that is shared by all tests, so use setUp and tearDown to reset to a known state, but only when the wrong state in the next test could be misleading.
To move away from globals, check whether the classes that need a global can share a common superclass, and if so pass the global to them on creation, since often fewer classes need it than feared.

Link Substitution in a procedural language like C creates a dummy library of same-signature functions to replace the real ones at link time, and for sensing you record each call in a global list or file to check later.

Link Substitution is most useful for faking external libraries that are mostly pure data sinks, which you call but whose return values you rarely care about, such as graphics libraries, and it also works in Java through same-named classes and classpath changes.

Parameterize Constructor externalizes an object created in a constructor by passing it in, and you can keep the original constructor signature delegating to the new one so clients do not have to change.

Parameterize Constructor's downside is that adding a parameter opens the door to further dependencies on that parameter's class, since clients can use the new constructor in production, though this is usually a small concern.

In languages with default arguments, Parameterize Constructor can just add a default argument to the existing constructor, but in C++ this forces the header to include the parameter's header and lose a forward-declaration opportunity, so use default arguments sparingly.
Parameterize Method passes an object the method creates internally in as a parameter, keeping a no-argument forwarding method for the original signature, so you can sense or separate.
When overloading a parameterized method with the same name as the original could confuse readers, name the new method after the parameter type instead, such as runWithTestResult.
Parameterize Method and Parameterize Constructor can make clients depend on new types at the interface, so when that is a concern, consider Extract and Override Factory Method instead.

Primitivize Parameter adds a free function that does the work on a simplified primitive representation, plus a class method that builds that representation and delegates, letting you add a tested feature when the class is too costly to instantiate.

Primitivize Parameter leaves code in a poor state by exposing the internal representation, adding untested glue, duplicating data, and deferring the real dependency-breaking, so only use it when you are confident you will bring the class under test later, and it is often a predecessor to Sprout Class.

Pull Up Feature moves a cluster of methods you want to test into an abstract superclass when the dependencies blocking instantiation are unrelated to that cluster, leaving the bad dependencies behind, and you then subclass the superclass for tests.
condition: when the blocking dependencies are unrelated to the methods you want to test

statement: Pull Up Feature spreads features across two classes for testability, which is less than ideal design; a better factoring is delegation to a dedicated object, but when that is too risky now, pulling up is a good first step made far less risky by Preserve Signatures and Lean on the Compiler.
Make a pulled-up superclass abstract so the code is easier to understand, because then every concrete class is known to be used and unused concrete classes stand out as apparent dead code.

Push Down Dependency makes the current class abstract, creates a production subclass holding the pervasive problematic dependencies such as UI calls, and subclasses the abstract class for testing; use it when dependencies are too pervasive for Subclass and Override Method or repeated Extract Interface.
condition: when problematic dependencies are pervasive rather than localized

statement: After Push Down Dependency, once tests exist you can pull shared logic back up and move the remaining environment-specific calls into a new class that ends up holding the only such dependencies.

Replace Function with Function Pointer in C declares a function pointer with the function's name, renames the original to a production name, and initializes the pointer to it, so tests can supply alternative definitions, providing a compile-time seam with minimal build impact.

Function pointers are seen as unsafe by some teams because their contents can be corrupted into calling random memory, and as a useful tool by others, and used with care they can separate dependencies that would otherwise be difficult or impossible.

Replace Function with Function Pointer yields seams usable to vary behavior in production, such as swapping the database, unlike Link Substitution whose seams you would not exploit in production, and you should consider upgrading a C project to C++ via mixed compilation for richer seams.

Replace Global Reference with Getter introduces a protected getter for each global used in a class, then uses Subclass and Override Method to return an appropriate object under test, or Extract Interface to break the dependency on the global's class.
A call to a static method on a class counts as a global reference for testing purposes, because the class itself is a global object that references state to do its work.

Subclass and Override Method is a core dependency-breaking technique that many others are variations of, using inheritance in a test to nullify behavior you do not care about or gain access to behavior you do.

A class's factoring determines how well inheritance can separate dependencies: a dependency isolated in a small method is easy to override, whereas otherwise you have to override a larger method to separate it.
Subclass and Override Method needs care: nulling out most of a method's behavior only makes sense when you do not care about that content for the specific thing you are testing right now.

The paper view is a mental model where, for almost any snippet in a method, extracting it to a method lets you replace it during testing, like laying a translucent overlay that swaps in different code for the parts you want to replace.
When using Subclass and Override Method, prefer overriding methods that already exist, because extracting methods without tests in place can be risky.

Subclass and Override Method requires making the target methods overridable (virtual in C++, non-final in Java, explicitly overridable in .NET) and adjusting visibility (Java and C# need at least protected, C++ can override private), and you should find the smallest set of methods to override.

Supersede Instance Variable adds a supersede method that destroys the previous instance and sets a new one, to replace an object created in a constructor when you must be able to swap it before another method runs.

C++ disallows constructor calls to overridden virtual functions, resolving them to the base version, because an override could access derived state not yet initialized, so Subclass and Override Method does not work for constructor-called virtuals there.

In C++, choose among constructor-dependency options by usage: Extract and Override Getter if the object is not used in the constructor, Supersede Instance Variable if it is used and must be replaceable before another method runs, and in languages that allow virtual calls in constructors, Extract and Override Factory Method is usually better.

Providing setters that change the base objects an object uses is generally poor practice, because they let clients drastically change behavior during the object's lifetime, forcing you to know its history, whereas code without such setters is easier to understand.
Naming a test-only mutator with an uncommon prefix like supersede lets you do a quick search to confirm it is not being used in production code.
Template Redefinition in C++ makes the class a template parameterized by the type you need to replace, with a typedef preserving the original name, then instantiates it on a fake type in the tests.

Template Redefinition's disadvantage is that templatizing moves implementation-file code into headers, increasing dependencies and forcing recompiles, so bias toward inheritance-based techniques and use Template Redefinition mainly when the dependency is already in templatized code.

Text Redefinition in an interpreted language such as Ruby redefines a method on the fly in the test file, with the downside that the redefinition persists until the program ends, so a forgotten redefinition can affect later tests.

Extract Method is perhaps the most useful refactoring: it systematically breaks large methods into smaller ones, making code easier to understand and enabling reuse to avoid duplication, and you use it to extract duplication, separate responsibilities, and break down long methods.

To extract a method safely you first need tests that thoroughly exercise it, then comment out the code, create an empty named method, call it, copy the code in, lean on the compiler for parameters and return values, adjust the signature, run the tests, and delete the commented-out code.
Comment out rather than delete the code you are about to extract, so that if a test fails you can easily revert to what you had and try again.

Coupling count is the number of values that pass in and out of a method when it is called: with no return value it equals the number of parameters, and with a return value it equals the number of parameters plus one.
A free function is a function that is not part of any class; in C it is just called a function, in C++ it is a non-member function, and such functions do not exist in Java and C#.
